Issued at 340 PM CDT FRI OCT 9 2026

Here is the latest on the forecast as the main focus once again
remains Hurricane Isaias. Changes to the forecast mainly deals
with the upgrade to the warnings (tropical and wind). We have
just slightly adjusted the timing to be a touch earlier, key
messages, and a reduced tornado potential. The slightly modified 
forecast discussion can be found below:

Hurricane Isaias Overview:

Hurricane Isaias is currently a Category 3 hurricane south of
Gulf Shores, Alabama. Isaias is expected to approach the U.S.
northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall tonight.
After landfall, it will undergo extratropical transition as it
turns northwestward, occludes, and merges into a deepening upper
low over Mississippi on Saturday. While the surface low quickly
weakens, an expanding wind field will overspread much of Central
Alabama into Saturday morning.

Tonight:

Conditions will rapidly deteriorate tonight. Widespread
precipitation will be present by early evening, with the
strongest winds occurring during the evening hours across the
southern half of the area. The peak wind impacts will materialize
after landfall and continue into Saturday morning. The sustained
tropical storm force wind probabilities may be conservative given
the pressure gradient with high pressure to the east, and do not
fully reflect the potential for damaging wind gusts. An
inversion/stable layer will remain in place north of a warm front
closer to the coast, though forecast soundings continue to
indicate significant winds near the surface. Highest sustained
winds are expected across southern counties, with higher wind
gusts of 50 to 60+ mph extending further north. Given the
anticipated impacts of widespread downed trees and power outages,
wind-related have been issued. With the transition to an extratropical
system, determining the exact boundary to transition from tropical
to non-tropical wind products remains challenging. Generally, I-20
in the east and I-22 serve as the approximate cutoff between 
tropical storm and high wind warnings. There is a possibility
after the system loses its tropical status, additional wind
advisories may be needed. 

High-resolution guidance indicates the heaviest rainfall will
occur during the evening and overnight hours across southern and
central Alabama. The heavy rain threat over West Alabama will be 
associated with the remnant core of the circulation evolving into 
a comma-head feature during extratropical transition. An 
additional north-to-south band of heavier rainfall is projected to
develop by Saturday morning, primarily across western Georgia but
potentially extending into far eastern Alabama. Lower rainfall 
totals are expected between these bands, but a Flood Watch remains
in effect for the entire area given the expected tropical 
rainfall and potential for localized flooding.

Regarding the tornado threat tonight, high-resolution guidance
remains consistent over the area north of the warm front,
suggesting the primary threat will be confined to early this
evening across the southeast. The warm front will be monitored
closely if it advances into Pike and Barbour Counties during the
pre-dawn hours, though the greater threat largely holds off until
after sunrise.

Saturday and Saturday night:

Gusty to localized damaging winds will continue across the area
Saturday morning. Wind speeds will gradually diminish from south
to north through the morning as the pressure gradient relaxes,
though conditions will remain gusty through the day due to
daytime mixing and enhanced wind fields aloft. A mid-level dry
slot will overspread the region, resulting in a general decrease
in widespread heavy rain, though shower activity and isolated
thunderstorms remain possible given abundant low-level moisture
and the proximity of the upper low. A band of heavier rain may
linger near the Georgia state line, with the highest totals
remaining in Georgia.

Instability trends will be monitored closely as the warm front
lifts northward Saturday morning, mainly for areas east of I-65,
while a developing cold or occluded front serves as the western
boundary for the severe threat. In general, instability will
increase as low-level shear and helicity decrease. However,
sufficient overlap of instability and shear may persist to
support an isolated tornado threat during the morning, though
indications suggest the primary north-to-south convective band
will have shifted into Georgia by that time. Into the afternoon
and evening hours, convective redevelopment will be evaluated, as
deep-layer shear along with marginal low-level shear could remain
supportive of isolated tornadoes.

Sunday onward:

Cloud cover and light rain or drizzle will linger on Sunday
before the upper low lifts out of the region. Beyond Sunday, dry
conditions return next week along with above-normal temperatures
as ridging builds over the area.
